newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO pleased, E.Europe relieved by summit result.
newsitem.headline: NATO pleased, E.Europe relieved by summit result.

text.p: NATO hailed the outcome of a U.S.-Russian summit on Friday as a major step towards a more secure and peaceful Europe and central European countries waiting to join the Atlantic Alliance voiced relief.

Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin agreed to differ at their Helsinki meeting on the eastward expansion of NATO, but said Moscow would nevertheless negotiate a partnership agreement with the alliance which they hoped all allied leaders would sign before a NATO summit in July.

Yeltsin reaffirmed Moscow's view that admitting ex-communist Warsaw Pact states to NATO would be "a serious mistake", but he chose instead to stress progress on arms control, NATO-Russia relations and Moscow's integration into international economic institutions.

Diplomats said the two leaders appeared to have made a tacit trade-off whereby Russia would neither bless nor actively fight NATO enlargement in exchange for a special economic and security relationship with the West and extra aid.
An official statement said NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, who is mandated to negotiate the NATO-Russia pact, was "especially encouraged" by Yeltsin's commitment to conclude a deal soon.
It said Solana saw many positive results of the summit but avoided saying what they were.

President Aleksander Kwasniewski of Poland, one of the leading candidates for NATO membership among former Soviet bloc allies, welcomed the outcome, saying Moscow had agreed de facto to NATO's expansion.
"In this basic question, in fact, I stress in fact, Russia has agreed on the expansion of NATO," Kwasniewski said in a statement to Reuters issued by his spokesman Antoni Styrczula.
"We also have the impression there was a drawing closer of standpoints and that in fact the expansion of NATO is decided," Kwasniewski said.
Earlier, the foreign ministers of the Czech Republic and Poland, meeting as the summit was proceeding, had warned against creating a tier of second class NATO members.

In a joint statement issued after talks at Rychnov Nad Kneznou, near the Czech-Polish border, the two nations also said those negotiations must not interfere with the schedule for admission of new members to the alliance.

"We trust that requirements for countries aspiring to alliance membership will result from direct accession negotiations and will not become part of any formal alliance obligations toward third countries, in order to avoid any second class membership," the statement said.
Gabor Szentivanyi, Hungarian foreign ministry spokesman, added: "NATO expansion is a sovereign decision of member states and those wishing to join."
Both Clinton and Yeltsin stressed that no European country should be treated unequally.

NATO has said it plans to invite the first central European candidates to begin membership negotiations at its July summit in Madrid with the aim of joining in time for the alliance's 50th anniversary in 1999.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are the leading candidates but several European NATO allies want Romania and Slovenia in the first wave of entrants.
"Yeltsin was never going to give its blessing to NATO's expansion, which would have been domestically disastrous, but both sides got what they wanted," one European diplomat said.
He said the remaining difficulties on NATO enlargement might be as much between Washington and some of its European allies as between the West and Moscow.
French President Jacques Chirac said on Thursday that all European countries had a right to join NATO eventually.
He did not say where the border should be but diplomats said there was a tacit understanding among most Western powers that no former Soviet republics would join the alliance.
That would satisfy Moscow's desire to keep the three Baltic republics -- Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia -- out of NATO.
